name: gradio-rag-pgvector
description: A start-GREEN Gradio chatbot that does retrieval-augmented generation over a REAL pgvector sibling service (Postgres + the vector extension). Deterministic stdlib embeddings (no model/network) so retrieval is reproducible + unit-testable; similarity search runs in pgvector. Proves the sibling-service path (design §5.6).
interface: core.generate_reply(message: str, history: list | None = None) -> str
knowledge:
The PoC answers ONLY from a FIXED, read-only corpus the scaffold ships as `core.CORPUS` — a Python list of documents, each a dict with `id`, `title`, and `content`. You CANNOT add facts to it; `generate_reply` retrieves from these documents via pgvector. The corpus covers four topics: (1) retrieval-augmented generation, (2) pgvector similarity search in Postgres, (3) grounded citations, (4) the Gradio chat interface. So a query about any of those topics has a matching document; a query about anything else (e.g. 'the weather on Mars', a made-up budget figure) matches nothing and yields the no-match reply.
CITATION FORMAT (do not guess it): the scaffold's `cite(doc)` returns the marker `[<id>]` where `<id>` is the document's INTEGER id, e.g. `[1]` or `[2]`. CORPUS ids are INTEGERS, not strings, and `generate_reply` emits that marker unchanged — the format is NOT `[doc-1]` or `[source:Title]`, so do not write a parser that assumes those.
TO PROVE REAL RETRIEVAL in a test (so it is not satisfiable by a constant stub): `from core import CORPUS`, build a query from words in a document's `title`, and call `generate_reply`. Assert the reply contains a `[N]` citation marker; then find WHICH document it cites by reading the integer between the square brackets (the digits inside `[...]`) and matching `next(d for d in CORPUS if d['id'] == int(N))` — compare the parsed id to `d['id']` as an INT (a string-vs-int mismatch is the classic unsatisfiable-test bug). Then assert a VERBATIM multi-word substring of THAT cited document's `content` appears in the reply — read the substring out of `CORPUS` at test time, never a literal you invent. Verifying the snippet against the cited doc (rather than a doc you pre-pick) makes the test robust to which document ranks first. For the negative/discrimination case, query an obviously unrelated string and assert the reply contains NO `[N]` citation marker (it is the no-match reply). Do NOT assert specific facts/values that are not present in `CORPUS`.
